newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti shares crash in panic selling.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti shares crash in panic selling.

text.p: Olivetti shares crashed to a new record low on Tuesday in a wave of panic selling as the Italian company scrambled to answer a battery of fresh questions from market regulators about the state of its finances.
Trading in the floundering information technology group shares plunged 9.91 percent to close at 465.3 lire after being halted repeatedly as they tested a 10 percent limit on price movements.

Investors have been in full retreat since Olivetti abruptly announced on Friday night that it was cancelling meetings between its chief executive officer Francesco Caio and financial analysts planned for this week in Milan and London.
"The stock is being treated like toxic waste," said a Milan-based investment banker who asked not to be named.

The sense of mounting crisis was reinforced by news on Monday that Caio was the target of a preliminary investigation by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its affairs.
In a further twist on Tuesday, judicial sources said both former chairman Carlo De Benedetti and his successor Antonio Tesone were also under preliminary investigation along with Caio.

"The cancellation of the meeting with Caio caused a crisis of confidence," said Michael Pacitti, an equities analyst at London-based brokerage James Capel. "That is only compounded by the investigation in Ivrea."

The financial community is anxious to question Caio about the group's performance and strategy because of growing doubts over the accuracy of Olivetti's first half results which revealed a loss of 440.2 billion lire ($289 million).

Olivetti has been engulfed by a dizzying succession of events in the past fortnight since De Benedetti was forced off the board after 18 years as chairman in a dramatic showdown with Caio, who formerly served as his personal assistant.
The company's shares, which at the beginning of the year stood at 1,280 lire -- nearly three times their present worth -- have lost almost one-third of their value since De Benedetti's resignation.

The biggest blow so far to the company's credibility came on September 4, the day after De Benedetti's dramatic exit, when Olivetti director general Renzo Francesconi resigned in a dispute with Caio over the first half results.

Stock market regulator Consob has questioned Caio and Francesconi over the results and on Monday night published a list of 16 questions about Olivetti's balance sheet and a demand for answers to be provided within 24 hours.
A spokeswoman for Olivetti said the company had hoped to issue a statement on Tuesday evening, but it would now aim to give its response on Wednesday morning at around 0600 GMT.
"At the moment there is a huge amount of uncertainty about the financial situation of the group and that won't go away until they answer the Consob questions," said Pacitti.
Some investors sharply criticised Consob, saying that Olivetti's shares should not be allowed to trade until the doubts over the true state of the company had been cleared up.

Investor doubts have focused on the true extent of Olivetti's financial exposure which has spiralled since the group completed a massive 2.26 trillion lire ($1.48 billion) rights issue at the end of last year.
The company said its net debt at the end of June totalled 1.26 trillion but analysts say that interest charges paid by the company suggest that it may really owe far more.
